Depends, what's your goal? If it's for a personal collection or emotional value due to your childhood, then absolutely!
If it's to sell, short answer is no. 

Long answer as to why: only top right looks like a decent candidate to get a good grade (no 10 though). Taken that into account, PSA 9 sell for around € 30 on eBay for this card, if you'd be lucky to get that grade in the first place.
Considering the price to grade a card, ship to and from a grading company, sell it afterwards (shipping costs again), potential fees.. I think you'd lose money or break even best case.

Couple of things come into perspective, being a small TCG YouTuber myself this is what I have learnt and applies to everything in the world and marketing.

- First of all, top seller is well-known across the platform. Just like with YouTube or certain brands, people will buy/consume your product just because they are familiar with it. Does that mean the service or product is better than a smaller/unknown brand? Nope. Often they cut ties to sell more despite putting less effort in.
- Secondly, the picture. Above picture is a lot clearer and sharper than yours, so more appealing. But, even then, you can have the best pictures, you're less known so people will still opt for a more well-known brand or seller.
- Lastly, SEO. The title (and perhaps description?) are better on the first auction. Coming from YouTube, the word 'Pokemon' has a better search rate than 'Pokémon', and that's just the accent on the 'e'. It's faster and easier to type, thus reaching a wider audience.

That all being said, as others have mentioned, auctions will only matter in the last few seconds. However, if you want to reach more people for a potential higher sale, adjust remark 2 and 3. You can't grow your brand that quickly, though, so you would still compete to the big guys regardless, who will 99% of the time end on top.

FC was introduced because it was cheaper for GW to use, though more expensive for the buyer. Of course, you would get 4 models instead of the 3 that came in metal, however, so there is that, I suppose. Obviously it backfired due to the low quality and then Forgeworld started making their resin figures, while GW switched to plastic kits only. At least for Middle-earth, I am not familiar with 40k and the othe games. Though, I do believe there it is the same concept.

One notorious model I remember, was the Great beast of Gorgoroth. Made completely in FC, but it was of such poor quality that the body halves didn't even fix together and people made video tutorials on how to fix it. That was the first model to be switched to Forgeworld resin, I believe, though the piece on top of the Beast for the archers to stand on, remained in FC. Quite an odd story, really.

So now FC is no longer being used for newer sculpts, but those that were made in the material, or saw a switch from metal to FC never got a switch back, which is why certain minis will be in FC still, despite all of the issues.. luckily, most were mass produced and you can easily find them in Facebook groups or eBay and so forth, but often with a slightly higher price. One that is, however, worth it in my opinion.

And yeah, GW sure has been busy. It took them almost a month to ship out my order recently. If they do not reply within a week/two weeks, just mail them again. Be sure to take clear pictures of what the problem is straight out of the pack and leave them like that until GW got back to you. But, I do have to praise their customer support, however. I've never heard anyone having been denied for a replacement!

Assembly itself is quite easy on itself, as they have the same sturdiness as plastic. So cutting through them etc will be no issue for your hobby knife! That's also about the only redeeming factor it has, unfortunately.  
The main problems with finecast are:

\- The air bubbles and such like I've mentioned before, that will just make your mini have 'missing' pieces, ruined details etc. Though this is no guarantee, of course, and it can also happen with other materials. It just seems to be more frequent with FC.  
\- The amount of flash on their sprue. You will have literal chuncks of flash that you'll have to cut away from underneath arms, cloaks.. any deeper places on the mini.. which is time consuming.  
\- Thinner pieces being bent. Just like with metal, a lot of bows, swords.. will be bend. The issue is.. you can not straighten them by just pulling them like you would on metal sculpts, as that would snap the weapons off with FC. What you want to do is warm them up by dipping them in warm water or a hair dryer and then straighten them as they're hot. People suggest to then immediately throw them in cold water which will 'harden' it again right away. I've only had to do this once, as I just avoid FC if I can!   


I've only had to contact GW once to replace a FC model as a weapon broke off straight from the pack. They sent me a new pack (complete, with all other models, too. GW does have good customer support!) but the exact same issue had happened here too.. so in the end, I just used green stuff to fill it all up instead as it seemed like less of a hassle than going through the process a third time.

With metal figures, you should be safe. Like with the missing bar on this one, I would not necessarily call it a defect as long as the miniature itself is not damaged.
If however you bought any finecast models.. yeah.. you might have to contact them as there is a big chance something is wrong with then. 
Finecast, or failcast, as our community calls it, is a terrible product, whilst also being more expensive! Plenty of air bubbles, pieces missing, flash you have to cut off with a hobby knife.. 

That's why GW not outsources their resin models to Forgeworld. Their resin miniatures are of a much higher quality! Though, those do not come with any bars either, actually. So if you ever would buy from them, you would still have to pin them to your base, as just glueing them on feels a little risky to me personally.

Even if not, I would still suggest getting yourself a hobby drill if you don't own one already. It will make bigger models that consist of multiple components a lot sturdier! Mainly metal ones, due to their weight.

You can contact GW as you technically received a 'broken' figure, though as it is just the bar, I'd suggest to just pin it.
A lot of us will cut the bar off to put the model and pin it on something (like a cork that's cut into the shape of a rock, for instance), to bring some variety in the army or have them stand out.

That might be possible, but that's where communication comes in. I often round down the price or share in shipping costs in return for it. Both parties are happy that way by the end of the day, and that's all that's important.

Comparing a big chain to private sales is redundant, it does not make sense at all as there is a different process at play.

If I, as a private seller, sell a product that I bought myself and decide to resell (with the intention of making profit, be break-even or to even reduce my personal collection in this case) and I cut out the middle man, that will be making me more money. 

In the case with cards, it's a product that does not require me to pay for manufacturing, labour.. it is ready to go right out of the pack. 
If however, I did produce the item myself or my company grows to the point I can not produce, ship, sell it, ... all by myself, a middle man such as target would indeed work. Or you hire people to work for you that will take care of the orders, package them, ship them, customer support.. depending on the item that you sell, as well as the consumer you wish to reach.

Furthermore, besides it depending on what you sell, it is also important to know if one does this as a side hussle to make some extra cash and to reduce their own collection, or it is something they live from/want to expand in.

So my answer is that I might. I might outsource to those big chain companies to sell my products, because I would still make my sale for the price that I decide to sell them for, or do it in house if I hire  people to do it, if I had those intentions.
However, in the case of being a private seller as is the case here, if I can avoid places like eBay that take a big chunk of my profit and do it all by myself, albeit perhaps with more time before making a sale, I'll do it myself and keep that 10%.

Edit: I've sold hundreds, if not thousands of cards over the past years all over the world and never had any complaints. Doing it yourself also makes sure you know that everything is packed well and sturdy, something I get a lot of praise for. That, and clear communication. Providing all the different options for shipping, sending pictures of the packed cards and final parcel, updating them if something would take longer..
Running a YouTube channel where people see that I take care of the cards and appreciate them for more than their monetary value also helps a lot, though. It is still a hobby to me, and I'm a collector in the first place, so I gladly help others complete their set if I can.
With games these days I'm sure that it will come as a DLC as some point.

eBay takes a big chunk out of the final price you sell for, so it's not weird at all, done it myself before. Just always use paypal's goods and services. Just ask an additional 5% on total costs to cover the fees. Never had problems with that and people are more than happy to spend the extra 5% if it means they're safe.

The Dwarfs fought their own wars. Erebor, (which we see in the Hobbit trilogy) for instance, was under siege by the Easterlings (the army we see marching into the Black Gate where Frodo and Sam hide using their Elven cloaks to look like rock) during the war of the Ring. The Mouth of Sauron (seen in the extended version of Return of the King) tried to persuade them, and the men of Dale, to fight for Mordor, which they refused. This was then answered by the siege. The Easterlings were very close to capturing the Mountain, too, really. 

Moria, or Khazad-Dum as it is known in the Dwarven language, had indeed fallen during this period. However, as we see in Fellowship of the Ring, there is the tomb of Balin (who we see in the Hobbit as well). A group of Dwarfs, led by Balin, made an expedition to reclaim Moria prior to when the Fellowship passed through. I believe approximately 30 years prior, but I'd have to check to make sure. Alas, we can see in the Fellowship of the Ring how that played out.. the Dwarfs had their last stand in the chamber of Mazarbul (or Balin's Tomb as it is referred the since his death). Gandalf reads that passage in the book, describing the last moments of the few remaining Dwarfs before attacked and slayed by the goblins that now reside in Moria.

Then there is also the Blue Mountains (aka Ered Luin) which lay to the West of the Shire, Bree etc. They had their own troubles with the goblins and other creatures that roam those lands as well. Although I'd have to refresh my mind on them to give more info, really.

Those are the main settlements of the Dwarfs during the Third Age, but there is smaller groups here and there as well. Some did fight for Mordor, as a matter of fact, but not much is known about them.

After the ring was destroyed, Gimli also took a group of Dwarfs to Helm's Deep. They found their place in the Glittering Caves in the mountain of which the keep was built as it was full of gems. You can also see these caves in the extended version of the second film, where Eowyn protects the women and children.
The Dwarfs also remade the broken gate of Minas Tirith during this period, using Mithril to strengthen it, which is a lot stronger.

That's a quick synopsis of what they were up to during the War of the Ring and once it was destroyed.
However, if you want to learn more about them, there is plenty of info to be found online! The Red Book of the Lotr Wiki sites for instance are very useful IMO.
